idiom_name: __getattr__/_getattribute__ forwarding hooks instead of listing every delegated method
implementation_notes: Python rarely needs the classic wrapper class per interface: defining `__getattr__` catches every attribute the wrapper does not define itself and `return getattr(self._inner, name)` forwards the rest, so the 'list every method' structure that delegation costs in Java or C++ disappears. `__getattribute__` is the escape hatch when the wrapper must also intercept names it defines, at the price of calling the base implementation to avoid infinite recursion. The same style lets a plain callable stand in for a single-method delegate; write explicit forwarding methods instead when the wrapper should expose a fixed, documented surface or when tooling (`dir`, `help`, type checkers) must see the members.
pitfalls: `__getattr__` fires only when normal lookup fails, so any attribute the wrapper happens to define - including typos and `self._inner` itself - silently shadows the delegate's member.

The forwarded attribute is bound to the delegate, not the wrapper: `self._inner.save` runs with `self` being the delegate, so overrides on the wrapper are not seen (write the wrapping method explicitly when that matters).

Forwarding hides the real API from introspection (`dir`, `help`, static type checkers) unless `__dir__` is defined, and it changes `copy`/`pickle` and equality semantics unless those are overridden too.
